paths.title: The Way of Peace
paths.description: From the greeting carried from house to house to the joy that does not depend upon events: two scenarios for learning peace as a practice, in a medieval village and in today's office.

paths.title: The Way of Simplicity
paths.description: What shall we do with the goods placed in our hands? Franciscan poverty as freedom from possession and as the responsibility of one who serves.

paths.title: The Way of Fraternity
paths.description: When a brother falls gravely, fraternity reveals what it truly is: tribunal or home. A path through forgiveness, rule, and mutual responsibility.

scenarios.title: The Boundary Wall
scenarios.situation: Assisi, early in the thirteenth century. Berta the dyer and Lupo the weaver dispute a strip of ground between their houses: the gutter passes there, and each swears the wall is on his side. Their families no longer greet one another. They both trust you. This evening they ask: whose side are you on?

options.text: Take neither side: listen to each of them, then to both together, and help them seek a plain agreement.
options.consequence: The first weeks are hard. In time they discover that the true knot is an old injury, not the strip of ground. The wall is settled, and the two workshops lend to one another again.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: Francis says in the Testament that the Lord revealed to him a greeting of peace to carry to others. Peace is not merely desired: it is delivered, person to person.

perspectives.label: The prudence of the village
perspectives.text: Mediation asks you to stand between two people without seeking gain. Your credibility is your only capital; spend it with care.

options.text: Send the matter before the consuls or the merchants' guild: measure the boundary and let the law decide.
options.consequence: A formal judgement assigns the wall and the gutter. The legal quarrel ends, but the old resentment remains under the ashes.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: A just judgement can settle the wall without restoring the bond. The greeting of peace seeks to place persons in relation again.

perspectives.label: The law of the commune
perspectives.text: A third party can end a feud without bloodshed or humiliation. This is a real civic good.

options.text: Do not intervene; refuse to feed the quarrel with judgements or gossip.
options.consequence: The tension lasts until winter rain floods both cellars. Shared need brings the neighbours back to speech, though some bitterness remains.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: Franciscan peace is active: it is carried and announced. Waiting may be humility, or it may be a convenient refusal to serve.

perspectives.label: The prudence of the village
perspectives.text: Not every conflict needs an early mediator; time and a common need can loosen a knot.

scenarios.closingReflection: Franciscan peace begins with a greeting and ends in a covenant guarded by the community. In your neighbourhood, who does this work—and could you do it?

scenarios.title: The Credit Taken
scenarios.situation: Today, before the whole team, a colleague presented as his own work that is largely yours. No one objected; the manager thanked him. Tomorrow you will meet his eyes again in the corridor.

options.text: Set the facts right publicly at the next opportunity.
options.consequence: The truth is restored, but the colleague becomes a lasting silent adversary and the team grows rigid.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: Perfect joy teaches that peace must not depend upon recognition. To restore the truth is lawful; to need applause in order to be at peace is another wound.

perspectives.label: The prudence of work
perspectives.text: Protecting one's work may be necessary. Correct the facts, never humiliate the person.

options.text: Let it go without nursing resentment; let the work speak in time.
options.consequence: Your peace returns, but the same behaviour is repeated with another colleague.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: Perfect joy receives an injury without giving it command of the heart. This is not weakness, but freedom.

perspectives.label: The responsibility of justice
perspectives.text: A wrong left unaddressed can become a habit and injure others. Peace of heart is not the only good.

options.text: Seek a sincere private conversation, state the facts without accusation, and listen.
options.consequence: The conversation is difficult but true. The colleague eventually names your contribution in the next meeting. You are not friends, but a vigilant respect begins.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: Going person to person resembles the greeting of peace: truth without a public tribunal, with the door left open.

perspectives.label: The prudence of work
perspectives.text: Private correction protects the facts without humiliating the person; if it fails, formal means remain.

scenarios.closingReflection: Perfect joy does not forbid restoring the facts; it forbids giving an injury the keys to your heart. How often is your peace rented out to another's behaviour?

scenarios.title: The Merchant's Trust
scenarios.situation: Assisi, 1210. Guido, a cloth merchant bound for the fairs of Champagne, asks you to guard bales of cloth and a purse of money for two years. You may use them and return their value with an agreed share of the profit. It is honest. It is also a bond that lasts two years.

options.text: Accept fully and use the goods to enlarge your workshop.
options.consequence: The workshop prospers, but every decision is now governed by the account you must render. You have spent two years guarding money more than living.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: The Rule asks the friars to appropriate neither house nor place nor anything: not because things are evil, but because what must be defended can begin to possess you.

perspectives.label: The merchant's logic
perspectives.text: Credit turns the economy. Risk can be measured, and honouring a pact builds a name.

options.text: Guard the goods without using them, and return them intact.
options.consequence: Your workshop remains small, but you walk lightly and Guido finds you a faithful man.

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: To guard without appropriating is to hold something in one's hands without holding it in one's heart.

perspectives.label: The prudence of the village
perspectives.text: Write the agreement before witnesses: trust is honoured by clarity.

options.text: Refuse with respect: give thanks for Guido's trust, but accept no bond of possession.
options.consequence: Your workshop remains modest, yet your word acquires a particular sound: that of one who is not for sale and not bound.

perspectives.label: The gaze of renunciation
perspectives.text: Francis returned even his clothes before the bishop, not from contempt for things but to be free to say "Our Father."

perspectives.label: The Franciscan way
perspectives.text: Freedom is not a rule made for oneself: the Rule speaks of not appropriating and of responsibility for what belongs to another.

scenarios.closingReflection: Franciscan poverty does not ask us to despise things. It asks us to notice when things begin to possess us. Who guards whom?

scenarios.title: The Opaque Project
scenarios.situation: You are offered a prestigious project with a chosen team and a substantial budget. Two expenses do not add up, and the funder answers with evasive courtesy. To sign is to accept responsibility for that opacity; to refuse is to lose a rare opportunity.

options.text: Accept without further questions: someone else would sign if you did not.
options.consequence: The project succeeds, but an audit later places your signature on the disputed accounts. The responsibility you refused to see reaches you.

perspectives.label: The servant's office
perspectives.text: A minister is a servant. A service that refuses to see what it answers for has already betrayed its name.

perspectives.label: The prudence of work
perspectives.text: Not every imperfection is corruption; responsibility begins by asking what one is signing.

options.text: Refuse at once and preserve your good name.
options.consequence: You lose the opportunity, while the project goes forward under another signature. You are safe, but the hidden matter remains hidden.

perspectives.label: The servant's office
perspectives.text: A servant must tell the truth even when it costs him a place.

perspectives.label: The prudence of work
perspectives.text: A refusal without asking for clarity can leave an honest question unanswered.

options.text: Pause the signature, ask for the records, and make the project conditional upon transparency.
options.consequence: The funder clarifies one account and withdraws the other. The project is smaller but clean, and your team trusts your service.

perspectives.label: The servant's office
perspectives.text: The one who serves bears responsibility without seeking glory; truth is part of the service.

perspectives.label: The prudence of work
perspectives.text: A clear condition protects both the project and the people who will carry it.

scenarios.closingReflection: A signature is a boundary: what you sign, you possess with its consequences. What are you willing to see before you serve?

scenarios.title: The Brother Who Fell
scenarios.situation: Ruffin, a brother entrusted with alms, has concealed part of the money and spent it. He confesses after the discovery. The village is scandalised; the fraternity is divided between severity and welcome.

options.text: Impose a public penance and send him to a distant hermitage.
options.consequence: The village sees discipline, but Ruffin departs humiliated and the brothers begin hiding their own frailties.

perspectives.label: The wisdom of community
perspectives.text: A common rule protects the weak and cannot become empty when someone falls.

perspectives.label: The Letter to a Minister
perspectives.text: Francis commands mercy even towards one who has fallen many times: severity must never become contempt.

options.text: Receive Ruffin without public penance, care for his illness, and answer scandal with meekness.
options.consequence: Ruffin remains and slowly returns to common life, but some in the village suspect the brothers of protecting their own.

perspectives.label: The Letter to a Minister
perspectives.text: Love more, not less, the one who has fallen; proclaim mercy, provided that he repents.

perspectives.label: The wisdom of community
perspectives.text: Mercy without truth becomes complicity; truth without mercy loses the brother.

options.text: Choose a communal path: Ruffin remains, restores what he can, and the fraternity accompanies the repair.
options.consequence: He returns the money house by house with an elder brother and serves humbly for a year. The village sees real repair, not humiliation; trust returns slowly.

perspectives.label: The Letter to a Minister
perspectives.text: Mercy is not a discount: it is love accompanying repentance until it bears fruit.

perspectives.label: The wisdom of community
perspectives.text: Brothers carry one another's needs. Communal repair joins truth and mercy.

scenarios.closingReflection: Fraternity is measured not when everyone keeps the rule, but when someone breaks it. Who finds a way back in your communities?

cards.title: The Greeting of Peace
cards.text: In the Testament Francis bears witness that the Lord revealed a greeting of peace to carry to others. Peace is not the absence of conflict: it is a gift delivered from house to house, person to person. The tradition of the wolf carries this logic to the edge: one goes towards what is feared. From it comes the popular formula "peace and good."

cards.title: Poverty as Freedom
cards.text: The Rule of 1223 asks the friars to appropriate nothing and to live as pilgrims and strangers in the world. Franciscan poverty does not glorify misery: it is freedom from being defined by possession. Its foundation is theological before it is economic: the Lord Himself became poor for us.

cards.title: Friars Minor
cards.text: Francis chose the name Friars Minor: no one is great, and those responsible are ministers, servants. Each brother must reveal his need, judge no brother, and not despise the weakness of the sick. Fraternity is daily responsibility, made concrete or not made at all.

cards.title: Brother Sun, Sister Water
cards.text: In the Canticle Francis praises God through and with the creatures: Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, and Sister Mother Earth. Nature is neither divinity nor warehouse: it is a family, because all creatures have one Father. The Canticle was composed in illness; praise does not depend upon circumstances.

cards.title: Perfect Joy
cards.text: In the Little Flowers Francis explains that true joy is not miracles or success, but returning rejected, cold, and mistreated, and remaining patient and glad. It is hagiographic narrative, not chronicle, yet it condenses an authentic Franciscan spirit: joy does not depend upon events.

cards.title: Seventy Times Seven, and Beyond
cards.text: In the Letter to a Minister Francis says that if a brother sinned a thousand times, he must still be loved and shown mercy, provided he repents. Franciscan forgiveness does not deny evil; it refuses to let evil have the final word over a relationship.

cards.title: Christmas at Greccio
cards.text: At Christmas 1223 Francis had a real manger prepared at Greccio, with hay, an ox, and an ass, so that the eyes of the body might see Bethlehem's poverty. Thomas of Celano presents it as a living memorial of the mystery, not a spectacle.

cards.title: The Meeting with the Sultan
cards.text: In 1219 Francis crossed the crusader lines at Damietta to meet al-Malik al-Kamil. Medieval sources remember a respectful dialogue amid irreducible difference of faith. In wartime, Francis chose an unarmed encounter.

cards.title: The Wolf of Gubbio
cards.text: The Little Flowers tell that Francis went towards the wolf that terrified Gubbio and spoke to it as to a brother. A covenant of peace followed. This is hagiographic tradition, precious for the Franciscan imagination rather than verifiable chronicle.

cards.title: Renunciation before the Bishop
cards.text: At the beginning of 1206 Francis returned his clothes and renounced his father's goods before Bishop Guido and Pietro di Bernardone. The bishop covered him with his mantle. It was public freedom from the idea of possession, not contempt for things.

cards.title: Clare of Assisi
cards.text: A noblewoman of Assisi, Clare left her father's house on the night of Palm Sunday 1212 to follow an evangelical form of life. She founded the Poor Ladies of San Damiano and defended the privilege of poverty. She was the first woman to write an approved religious rule for women.

cards.title: Bernard of Quintavalle
cards.text: A wealthy citizen of Assisi, Bernard became Francis's first companion. He distributed his goods to the poor and chose the itinerant life. Without the first brother, there is no fraternity.

cards.title: Brother Leo
cards.text: Francis's companion and confessor in his final years, Leo was witness at La Verna and keeper of the saint's autograph. Francis answered his anxiety with freedom: follow your conscience before God.

cards.title: Sultan al-Malik al-Kamil
cards.text: The Ayyubid sultan received Francis at Damietta in 1219. Their encounter converted neither man; it showed that believers can speak without weapons in hand.

cards.title: The Medieval Commune
cards.text: Francis's Assisi was a rising commune of consuls, podestà, towers, feuds, merchants, and guilds. It was a world of honour, rank, and credit, where poverty was shame. The Franciscan choice took shape against the power possession exerted upon the heart.

cards.title: The Leprosarium
cards.text: In the thirteenth century lepers lived outside the walls, excluded from civic life. Francis writes in the Testament that seeing them seemed bitter, and that among them the Lord led him to show mercy and find sweetness. Charity is not a feeling but an encounter of bodies.

cards.title: Almsgiving
cards.text: The Rule asks the friars to go for alms without shame, remembering that the Lord became poor. Asking becomes part of life, not a humiliation. Giving becomes relationship: one does not leave something with the poor, one remains with the poor.

cards.title: The Hermitage
cards.text: Franciscan life is not only road and preaching. Francis sought solitary retreats—at the Carceri and La Verna—where long silence returned him to the essential. Retreat and mission are the two feet of the road.

cards.title: What Possesses You?
cards.text: Make an inventory of what you value most. Ask, one by one: do I possess it, or does it possess me? How much of your time and anxiety serves to defend what you have? There is no correct answer, only truth about you.

cards.title: Who Is Your Wolf?
cards.text: In your neighbourhood, work, or family, who is the person from whom everyone flees? What would happen if someone went towards them and asked: what are you hungry for?

cards.title: What Does Your Joy Depend Upon?
cards.text: Think of your last deep gladness. Did it depend upon achievement, recognition, or purchase? Now seek a joy no outward event can take away. What must change within you for joy not to be rented from events?

cards.title: The Way of Peace
cards.text: Two scenes: a boundary quarrel in a medieval village and an injury suffered in today's office. Franciscan peace is a greeting to carry, a mediation to offer, and a joy not held hostage by events.

cards.title: The Way of Fraternity
cards.text: A path through common life: what happens when a brother falls and the community divides between severity and welcome? Franciscan fraternity is measured precisely there.
